intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome-4 (CAMRQ4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ATP8A2 gene on chromosome 13q12.

paragraphs.text: Cerebellar ataxia, impaired intellectual development, and dysequilibrium syndrome (CAMRQ) is a genetically heterogeneous, early-onset neurodevelopmental condition characterized by nonprogressive cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability of varying severity, and cerebellar atrophy; other possible features include severe hypotonia, delayed motor development, dysarthria, seizures, optic atrophy, and short stature, and quadrupedal locomotion has been seen in a few patients (summary by Mohamadian et al., 2020). The phenotypic spectrum of CAMRQ4, caused by ATP8A2 mutation, is broad, ranging from congenital ataxia with near-normal cognition (Damasio et al., 2021) to severe developmental delay with involuntary movements and visual and hearing impairment (Narishige et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Mohamadian et al. (2020) reported 3 sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent with nonprogressive cerebellar ataxia, severe hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria, and cerebellar atrophy. The proband, a 9-year-old girl born to healthy first-cousin parents, had normal weight, height, and head circumference at birth after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her first sign was severe neonatal hypotonia, followed by delay of all psychomotor and developmental milestones. She was wheelchair-bound and could not walk, sit, or hold her head, and had had feeding difficulties since infancy. Her affected brother and sister, aged 17 and 15 years, had similar features. All 3 patients had IQ levels ranging from 20 to 40, delayed speech and language with dysarthria, and absent deep tendon reflexes; hearing examination showed no significant impairment. Metabolic investigations were normal, and brain MRI showed cerebellar atrophy in all patients. The authors' comparison table recorded onset at birth, no seizures, and no optic atrophy in these patients.

paragraphs.text: Damasio et al. (2021) described 2 sibs with congenital ataxia who acquired independent gait by 4 years of age. After 16 years of follow-up, they had near-normal cognition, cerebellar ataxia, mild pyramidal signs, and dystonia. The authors concluded that ATP8A2-related disorders include less severe forms of congenital ataxia.

paragraphs.text: Narishige et al. (2022) reported Japanese sibs who presented with athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development. One patient had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Flattening of the auditory brainstem responses and areflexia developed. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or achieve head control, although some nonverbal communication was preserved. The symptoms did not progress in the early period of development, and the authors noted that the disorder may be difficult to distinguish from dyskinetic cerebral palsy, particularly in solitary cases.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of CAMRQ4 in the families reported by Onat et al. (2013) and Mohamadian et al. (2020) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance: in each consanguineous family, affected sibs carried a homozygous ATP8A2 variant, and in the family of Mohamadian et al. (2020) both parents were heterozygous carriers. Narishige et al. (2022) found compound heterozygous ATP8A2 variants in affected sibs.

paragraphs.text: Ozcelik et al. (2008) studied 4 large consanguineous Turkish kindreds with quadrupedal gait, dysarthric speech, mental retardation, and cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia. Mutations in the VLDLR gene were found in 2 families, whereas in the 2 other families the phenotype was not linked to chromosome 9p, indicating that hereditary disorders associated with quadrupedal gait in humans are genetically heterogeneous. Gulsuner et al. (2011) identified a mutation in the WDR81 gene in a consanguineous Turkish family with quadrupedal locomotion, mental retardation, and cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia, and noted that WDR81 was the third gene, after VLDLR and CA8, implicated in quadrupedal locomotion in humans. Onat et al. (2013) described cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, and dysequilibrium syndrome as rare and heterogeneous.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ4, Onat et al. (2013) identified a missense mutation (I376M) in the ATP8A2 gene. The mutation was found by targeted next-generation sequencing of an affected individual, followed by segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction approaches; it lay in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1-E2 ATPase domain. The authors noted that ATP8A2 is expressed mainly in brain, particularly cerebellum. In a later comparison table, Mohamadian et al. (2020) listed this mutation as homozygous c.1128C-G.

checks.explanation: The variant was found in the consanguineous Turkish family. Using the name CAMRQ4 is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: In 3 sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4, Mohamadian et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene, resulting in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution. The mutation, which was found by whole-exome sequencing of the proband after normal karyotype and chromosomal microarray analysis, was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with the disorder: the parents, a healthy brother, and a healthy sister were heterozygous, and another healthy sister was wildtype. It was not found in public variant databases or in 100 healthy ethnically matched controls. The residue lies in a highly conserved region of the ATP-binding domain, and in silico analysis and structural modeling predicted reduced protein stability and an effect on the ligand-binding pocket.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with a mild form of CAMRQ4, Damasio et al. (2021) identified a homozygous intronic variant (c.1580-18C-G) in intron 17 of the ATP8A2 gene by exome sequencing. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the variant created an alternative acceptor splice site, producing an aberrant transcript that retained 17 bp of intron 17 and was predicted to result in a premature stop codon after insertion of 4 amino acids.

paragraphs.text: In 3 sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4, Mohamadian et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene, resulting in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution at a highly conserved residue. The mutation, found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, segregated with the disorder in the family and was not found in 100 ethnically matched controls. Structural modeling predicted reduced protein stability and an altered ligand-binding pocket.

agent.process_note: I opened all 9 papers. Mohamadian et al. (2020) was the only full text, and I read all of it. Five papers were available as abstracts only (Ozcelik 2008 on VLDLR, Gulsuner 2011 on WDR81, Onat 2013, Damasio 2021 and Narishige 2022). Three were title only (the Humphrey, Herz and Ozcelik 2008 correspondence), so I did not cite them. The Onat abstract does not give the nucleotide change or the zygosity of I376M. I took both (homozygous c.1128C>G) from Mohamadian's comparison table and credited that table in the text. The ancestry of the Damasio sibs and the first report of R581X are not in the available texts. No gene MIM number was supplied, so I left it out; the 13q12 location comes from Onat's mapping and Mohamadian's text. Discrepancies left out: Mohamadian reports a 46,XY karyotype for a female proband, and writes both G447R and G477R. Papers on VLDLR and WDR81 were used only for the heterogeneity section.
